title: The conditions on a loan follow the largest shareholders' preferences as well as the borrower's numbers
conviction: Two published studies and the two lenders' own voting tables. Nothing on this map's own cases has been matched against either.
summary:
Both main development lenders are companies with shareholders, and the shares are not equal. The International Bank for Reconstruction and Development's own table of subscriptions and voting power, data as of 30 June 2026, gives 2,918,202 votes across 189 countries. The United States holds 466,319 of them, 15.98 per cent. Japan holds 6.88 per cent, China 5.75 per cent, Germany 4.09 per cent, France and the United Kingdom 3.75 per cent each. The IMF's Annual Report 2025 gives the same picture for the Fund as of 30 April 2025: the United States casts 831,394 votes, 16.49 per cent of the total, Japan 6.14 per cent and China 6.08 per cent.

Those percentages matter because of the thresholds written into the IMF's Articles of Agreement. The index to the Articles lists 22 kinds of decision that require an eighty-five per cent majority of the total voting power, including adjustment of quotas, the creation of the Council, the number of Executive Directors, and compulsory withdrawal of a member. Article XXVIII(a) requires, for any amendment to the Agreement, that three-fifths of the members holding eighty-five per cent of the total voting power accept it. A single member holding more than 15 per cent can therefore block each of those decisions on its own, without needing an ally.

What gets attached to a loan has been counted. Kentikelenis, Stubbs and King searched 4,590 loan-related documents for 1985 to 2014 and extracted 55,465 individual conditions across 131 countries; the median number of conditions applying per year was about 42 over 1996 to 2007 and 44 in 2014. Dreher and Jensen read 206 letters of intent from 38 countries signed between April 1997 and February 2003 and set the number of conditions in each against how often that country voted the same way as the United States in the UN General Assembly. Moving a country from never voting with the United States to always voting with it reduced the number of conditions by about three. Prior to elections, countries not voting with the United States carried more structural benchmarks and closer allies carried fewer.
implications: If it holds, a condition is partly a price set by the shareholders rather than a remedy drawn from the borrower's accounts, and two loans with the same economic numbers can carry different conditions. It would also mean that the thresholds in the Articles are not only about amendments: a member that can block a quota change can also make its views expensive to ignore in an ordinary programme discussion. For this map it would mean that the conditions recorded on a case are evidence about the lender's shareholders as well as about the borrower.
missing: No case on this map has had its conditions matched against the borrower's UN voting record or against what the largest shareholders asked for. The two studies stop in 2003 and 2014, so nothing covers the programmes of the last decade. The Executive Board's own discussion of a programme is not on the map in any form.
would_refute: A recount of the 55,465 conditions, or of the programmes agreed since 2014, finding no relation between the number or kind of condition and the borrower's voting alignment once the borrower's own economic figures are held constant. That would make the 1997 to 2003 result a feature of one period.
would_settle: The Executive Board minutes and room documents for a run of programme approvals, read beside the United States Treasury's annual report to Congress, which records how the US Executive Director voted and what policies it pressed for. Matching those votes and requests case by case against the conditions in each letter of intent would show whether the two move together.

countries.role: Largest shareholder in both lenders
countries.note: 15.98 per cent of IBRD voting power, 466,319 of 2,918,202 votes, as of 30 June 2026. 16.49 per cent of IMF voting power, 831,394 votes, as of 30 April 2025. Above the 15 per cent needed to block each of the 22 decisions the IMF Articles put behind an 85 per cent threshold.

countries.note: 6.88 per cent of IBRD voting power and 6.14 per cent of IMF voting power.

countries.note: The 2023 and 2024 revenue-measure cases turn on tax conditions in a live IMF arrangement. Neither has been set against Kenya's voting record.

looked_at: The two lenders' current voting tables, the IMF Articles of Agreement including its index of special majorities, and two peer-reviewed studies of conditionality. No work on this map's own cases.

title: A small circle of arbitrators decides most of the claims companies bring against states
conviction: One 2012 count over 450 cases and one register's figures for 2025. The 2012 count has never been redone against the 1,332 cases now known.
summary:
UNCTAD's dispute settlement register lists 1,332 known investor-state claims, with 133 states appearing as respondent. The tribunals that decide them are appointed case by case, usually three arbitrators, and there is no fixed bench.

In 2012 the Transnational Institute and Corporate Europe Observatory counted who had sat on them. Of 450 investment-treaty disputes known at that date, 15 arbitrators had decided 247, which is 55 per cent. On the larger claims the share was higher: 79 of 123 disputes worth at least US$100 million, 64 per cent, and 12 of 16 disputes worth at least US$4 billion, 75 per cent. The same report counted three law firms, Freshfields, White & Case and King & Spalding, claiming involvement in 130 investment-treaty cases in 2011 alone.

The repetition is still visible in the one register that publishes its own figures. ICSID had 1,085 cases registered under its Convention and Additional Facility rules as of 31 December 2025. In 2025 it recorded 240 appointments of arbitrators, conciliators and ad hoc committee members, covering 49 nationalities, and 13 per cent of those appointments were of someone sitting on an ICSID case for the first time. The other 87 per cent went to people who had sat before. Nationals of Western European countries took 38 per cent of the 2025 appointments, the largest single regional group, and South American nationals 20 per cent.
implications: If the concentration still holds across all 1,332 claims, then the rule a treaty means in practice is set by a group small enough to know each other, and a state facing a claim is facing people who will hear the next one too. It would also mean that a reform aimed at treaty text leaves the deciding unchanged, because the same people would read the new text. For this map it would mean the arbitration cases on the cards are not separate events but repeat appearances.
missing: Nobody has recounted the 2012 figure. UNCTAD's register names the arbitrators in most cases, and ICSID publishes its tribunals, but no count by arbitrator across the 1,332 claims has been made here. The map holds 4 cases against those 1,332, so this map's own arbitration cases are far too few to count anything from.
would_refute: A count of arbitrator names across all 1,332 known claims showing the fifteen busiest now account for well under a third, and the first-time appointment rate rising. The ICSID register alone would show the second half of that.
would_settle: A full count of arbitrator names in the UNCTAD register and the ICSID case list, broken down by who appointed each one and by the size of the claim, repeating the 2012 method on the current caseload.

countries.role: Two claims after cancelled contracts
countries.note: The Cochabamba water concession went to an ICSID tribunal about 18 months after the contract was cancelled. The 1997 pension privatization card also records a claim.

countries.note: Bear Creek's Santa Ana claim followed the Aymarazo protests, and the La Oroya smelter card records a Renco claim.

countries.note: Eco Oro brought a claim over the Angostura project in the Santurbán páramo.

countries.role: Claim after a refused mine permit
countries.note: Gabriel Resources brought a claim over Roșia Montană.

countries.role: Claims running both ways
countries.note: The Perenco card records a tribunal that made its own pollution finding; the Chevron card records a treaty claim against the state after a domestic judgment.

looked_at: UNCTAD's register totals, the 2012 TNI and CEO count, and ICSID's published 2025 caseload figures. No new counting.

title: Committees with no published membership decide how much a country can spend for a decade
conviction: The official creditors' own totals and one campaign group's attempt to name the private ones. No count of committee membership exists to check.
summary:
When a country cannot pay, the terms it gets are agreed in committees of its creditors. On the official side the Paris Club says it has 22 permanent members and gives totals of 484 agreements with 102 debtor countries covering US$616 billion of debt. It names its permanent members. Its decisions are reached among those 22 and the debtor is not one of them.

On the private side the committee cannot be named at all, because the holders cannot be named. Debt Justice and Christian Aid tried in December 2025 for the bonds of 15 lower-income countries and wrote that there is no publicly accessible information on who owns bonds; the paid data they used, from Refinitiv, covered 23 per cent of the ownership of those bonds. They also found 99 per cent of those bonds governed by English law, and 63 per cent of the 15 countries' external debt to private creditors owed as bonds. So the body that agrees how much of a bond debt is written off is assembled from holders whose identity is known for less than a quarter of the paper.

What the committees agree sets the borrower's budget for years. On this map, Zambia's 2020 default, Sri Lanka's 2022 missed payment and Mozambique's hidden loans each run through a creditor process whose participants are only partly on the record. In Zambia's case the map already records a bondholder committee estimated to hold about 45 per cent of the country's international market debt, named only by its chair.
implications: If the membership is routinely unpublished, then a country's spending room for a decade is set in a room whose occupants cannot be listed, and nobody outside can check whether the same funds sit on successive committees. It would also mean that comparing one restructuring with another is guesswork, because the counterparties are not known to be the same or different. For this map it would mean that a card describing a restructuring can name the terms but not the people who set them.
missing: No register of creditor committee membership has been looked for, and none is known to exist. The official creditor committees formed under the G20's Common Framework have not been checked for published membership. Nothing on this map counts how many of its debt cases went through a committee at all.
would_refute: Membership lists for the official creditor committees and the bondholder committees turning out to be published, or a regulator's holdings register showing that ownership is in fact recorded and obtainable. Either would mean the committees are documented and the suspicion is about reading, not secrecy.
would_settle: The membership lists and minutes of the official creditor committees formed under the Common Framework, together with the bondholder committee membership in a handful of restructurings, set against a holdings register. Repeat appearances across countries would show whether the same creditors sit on each.

countries.role: Default with a committee named only by its chair
countries.note: The 2020 Eurobond default card records a bondholder committee estimated to hold about 45 per cent of Zambia's international market debt, and all private lenders except one refusing the September 2020 request to suspend payments.

countries.role: Default with one holder identified by a lawsuit
countries.note: Hamilton Reserve Bank, holding more than US$250 million of bonds, became known only because it sued in New York in June 2022.

countries.role: Debt contracted outside the published record
countries.note: More than US$2 billion was borrowed through special companies on purported state guarantees; the English High Court found in 2024 that the debt was procured by bribery and corruption.

looked_at: The Paris Club's own key figures and permanent membership page, and the December 2025 Debt Justice and Christian Aid report on the bonds of 15 countries.

title: Two private committees decide which countries investors may lend to
conviction: One peer-reviewed study of index inclusion from 1990 to 2015, one regulator's market-share table, and one UN agency's estimate. No test against this map's cases.
summary:
Most money that buys a developing country's bonds is not choosing that country. It is tracking an index. Cormier and Naqvi studied inclusion in JP Morgan's Emerging Market Bond Index Global from 1990 to 2015 and report a World Bank estimate that 70 per cent of mutual fund investments, and over 50 per cent of active portfolio investments, in the emerging market sovereign bond market are explained by the composition of that one index. At least US$306 billion of assets formally tracked it in 2018. Its country coverage went from 14 countries at its creation in 1993 to 38 at the end of 2007 and 72 by January 2019. Inclusion turns on a short list of criteria set by JP Morgan: a national income threshold, a credit rating threshold and a minimum bond size.

One of those criteria is another private decision. The European regulator's own market-share table for 2024 puts S&P Global Ratings at 47.81 per cent, Moody's at 30.59 per cent and Fitch at 11.86 per cent, so three firms hold 90.26 per cent of the registered market there. A rating action by one of them can therefore move a country across an index threshold, and the money follows the threshold rather than the country.

What the ratings cost borrowers has been estimated. The UNDP's April 2023 study of sovereign credit ratings in Africa found up to US$74.5 billion could be saved if ratings rested on less subjective assessment. The study's own framing is that part of a rating is judgement rather than measurement, and judgement is made in a committee whose deliberations are not published.
implications: If it holds, then the decision that opens or closes a country's access to private lending is made by a committee at a bank or a rating firm, not by the investors whose money moves and not by any public body. It would also mean that a country can do everything its lenders asked and still lose access because a threshold moved. For this map it would mean that the defaults and payment crises on the cards have an earlier step that no card records.
missing: No case on this map has had the dates of its index inclusion or exclusion, or its rating actions, set against the dates money arrived or left. The index study ends in 2015 and the market-share table covers the European Union only, not the world. Nobody has checked whether the index rules were applied mechanically or with discretion in any single instance.
would_refute: The index rules turning out to be applied mechanically, with no committee discretion in any inclusion or exclusion, together with a finding that inclusion has no effect on the volume of lending once a country's rating and its own figures are held constant. That would make the index a thermometer rather than a switch.
would_settle: The index provider's committee records for a set of inclusions and exclusions, and the rating committees' records for the sovereign actions that crossed the index threshold, set against the dated capital flow figures for those countries.

countries.role: Default following rating and market exit
countries.note: The 2020 Eurobond default card records private lenders refusing a payment suspension. Neither the rating actions nor the index treatment that preceded it are on the card.

countries.role: Payment default and a bondholder suit
countries.note: The 2022 card records the missed payment and the New York suit, with no record of the rating or index steps before it.

countries.role: Borrower with 16 cases and no rating record on them
countries.note: Ghana appears 16 times on this map through projects and protests. No card records an index or rating decision.

looked_at: One study of EMBIG inclusion, the European regulator's 2024 market-share calculation, and the UNDP's 2023 press statement of its Africa ratings study.

title: Bodies with no treaty and no vote set rules that cut a country off from the banking system
conviction: One standard-setter's own charter and one IMF study of 89 countries. The listings have not been matched against anything on this map.
summary:
Some of the rules that decide whether money can cross a border are written by bodies that are not founded on a treaty and take no vote of the countries they affect. The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision says so in its own charter: "The BCBS does not possess any formal supranational authority" and "Its decisions do not have legal force." The same charter says the Committee "expects full implementation of its standards by BCBS members and their internationally active banks" and expects them written into national law within a timeframe the Committee sets.

The measurable version of the effect is the Financial Action Task Force's grey list, formally the list of jurisdictions under increased monitoring. An IMF working paper by Kida and Paetzold studied capital flows in 89 emerging and developing countries over 2000 to 2017 and found that grey-listing cuts a country's capital inflows by 7.6 per cent of GDP on average. The same paper summarises an earlier study using SWIFT data on cross-border payments between 2004 and 2014, which found that being added to the grey list reduced the number of payments sent to the affected country by the rest of the world by 7 to 10 per cent. When the paper was written 19 countries were on the grey list and two, Iran and North Korea, on the blacklist.

Neither list is a sanction imposed by any treaty body. The mechanism the paper describes is banks ending relationships to cut compliance costs, and investors using the listing as a shorthand for risk.
implications: If it holds, a decision taken in a body with no treaty and no borrower vote can do more to a country's access to money than any loan condition, and it can be taken without a hearing the country can appeal. It would also mean that the lenders' conditions are not the only rules a borrower has to meet, and that a card describing a country's loss of access may be describing a listing rather than a lending decision. The effect size, 7.6 per cent of GDP, is larger than most of the loan amounts on this map.
missing: Nobody has set grey-listing dates against the cases on this map, although at least eight countries with cases here have been listed. The decision records of these bodies have not been looked for. The IMF study's own caution, that there are few listing events to work with, has not been tested against a longer run of data.
would_refute: The 7.6 per cent effect disappearing in a larger sample, or once an IMF programme and a ratings change over the same months are held constant. That would make the listing a marker of trouble rather than a cause of it.
would_settle: The plenary records showing how a particular listing decision was taken, who proposed it and what the listed country was allowed to say, set against dated bank-exit and payments data for the months either side.

countries.note: On the grey list at the time of the IMF study. No card here records the listing or what it did to the money.

title: Commodity traders lend against future output on terms almost nobody can read
conviction: One counted dataset of 52 loans. Seven of them are trader loans, which is few, and the dataset's authors say it is incomplete.
summary:
A state short of money can borrow against oil or minerals it has not produced yet. The Natural Resource Governance Institute counted the deals it could find: 52 resource-backed loans signed between 2004 and 2018 in sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America, agreed by 14 countries, worth US$164 billion, of which US$66 billion was taken by sub-Saharan African countries and US$98 billion by Latin American ones. Chinese policy banks were the lender in 38 of the 52. Commodity traders were the lender in seven, Chinese state-owned enterprises in four, and the Export-Import Bank of Korea, the Nigerian government and Rosneft in one each. Forty-three of the 52 were backed by oil.

The figure that makes this a suspected pattern rather than a finding is a disclosure count. The report says the loan agreement is publicly available in only one of the 52 cases, the Sicomines deal in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and that every other loan it identified is missing key terms. It says that on oil advances specifically, commodity traders "are just as opaque as other lenders" and generally make substantial disclosures only when repayment problems emerge. It notes that traders bring banks in behind them: Deutsche Bank, Crédit Agricole and ING partly financed Glencore's loan to Chad.

This map already documents the Chinese state version of the same shape in the pattern on secrecy and security in Chinese loan contracts, where 100 contracts were published and found to carry confidentiality clauses and lender-controlled revenue accounts. The trader version has no equivalent published set of contracts at all.
implications: If it holds, a share of a country's future export earnings is committed under terms no citizen, parliament or other creditor can read, and the lender is a trading company rather than a bank or a state. It would also mean that a country's published debt figures understate what is owed, because an advance against future cargoes may not appear as debt. For this map it would mean that the austerity and seizure cases in oil-exporting countries have a contract behind them that cannot be obtained.
missing: The map holds no case where a trader prepayment is the mechanism on the card. The 52-loan dataset stops in 2018 and its authors say it is not comprehensive and may not be representative. Nobody has looked at the debt registers of the 14 countries to see which advances they list.
would_refute: The agreements being obtained for a reasonable number of the deals and turning out to carry ordinary syndicated lending terms, with the security and interest rates no less visible than in a bond prospectus. The borrowing states' own debt registers would show much of that.
would_settle: The loan agreements themselves, or the borrowing states' published debt registers listing each advance with its interest rate, maturity, security and the volume of output pledged. A count of how many of the deals appear in each country's official debt figures would show whether the money is recorded at all.

countries.role: Oil revenue already seized by other creditors
countries.note: The card on debt funds seizing Congo-Brazzaville's oil revenue records creditors holding under US$500 million blocking the country's oil exports for years. The NRGI report records Congo releasing extra information on its advances in late 2018 alongside an IMF programme.

countries.role: Trader loan behind an austerity crisis
countries.note: Glencore lent to Chad against oil, with Deutsche Bank, Crédit Agricole and ING partly financing it. The map carries the 2018 anti-austerity protests and a Glencore oilfield wastewater case, neither of which records the loan terms.

countries.role: Largest recipient of resource-backed loans in the dataset
countries.note: Angola received the largest amount of resource-backed loans in the NRGI dataset, including trader loans. The map's four Angolan cases are fuel protests and projects, none of them about the loans.

countries.role: The one deal whose agreement is public
countries.note: Sicomines is the single case of the 52 where the loan agreement is publicly available, following an EITI disclosure request.

looked_at: The NRGI report Resource-Backed Loans: Pitfalls and Potential, including its dataset description and its section on transparency.

title: About half the money a development lender puts out goes through a bank, and the end borrower is not named
conviction: One compliance audit and one campaign report, both about a single lender and both at least nine years old.
summary:
A development lender can lend to a project or it can lend to a bank that lends to projects. The second kind leaves no public record of where the money ended up. The Compliance Advisor Ombudsman's audit of October 2012 found that financial-market activities were "over 40 percent of IFC's portfolio, and the proportion has been growing." The same audit found that the lender was unable to measure whether the environmental and social management system it requires of the bank worked at the sub-client level, and that people affected by a sub-client's project "may not know about IFC's relationship to the subclient transaction, or about the CAO as an available recourse mechanism." It took a 10 per cent sample of 737 projects, and said in terms that the sample was not statistically representative.

Inclusive Development International counted the same portfolio in 2016. It found long-term investments in financial intermediaries up 45 per cent between the 2010 and 2015 financial years and making up roughly 50 per cent of the lender's long-term commitments in 2015, a share that would rise if short-term trade finance were included. In that year the lender put US$507 million into funds and more than US$4.5 billion into financial markets, which is why the report puts around 90 per cent of its intermediary business in the part where no sub-client is named. Private equity funds, the one part whose investments the lender had agreed to disclose, were 6 to 10 per cent of the intermediary portfolio.

Two cards on this map reach a sub-client. One records a palm oil and plantation group identified through its bank financiers; the other records coal plants financed through a bank. Both were found by someone tracing the chain backwards, not from any published list.
implications: If it holds, then for roughly half of one lender's money there is no list of the projects it paid for, and a person harmed by one of them has no way of knowing a development lender is behind it. It would also mean that the complaint registers this map relies on cannot cover that half, because a complaint requires knowing who financed you. For this map it would put a floor under the thinness noted in the suspected pattern on missing registers: for intermediary lending there is no list to work from at all.
missing: Both sources are about one lender, and the newer is from 2016. The current share of intermediary lending has not been counted, and no equivalent count has been made for the other development lenders, the regional banks or the bilateral development finance institutions. Nobody has counted how many of this map's cases were financed through an intermediary rather than directly.
would_refute: A published list of sub-clients covering most intermediary lending, showing that the end borrowers are in fact named. The lender's own disclosure portal would settle that in one reading.
would_settle: The sub-client lists held in the lender's supervision files, with a count of how many are named publicly and how many are not, for a single financial year. Repeating the count for two or three other development lenders would show whether the share is general.

countries.role: Sub-client reached by tracing the financiers
countries.note: The Indofood and London Sumatra card names the banks behind the group. It exists because someone traced the chain, not because a list was published.

countries.role: Coal plants financed through a bank
countries.note: The RCBC coal plants card records power stations reached through a bank rather than a direct project loan.

looked_at: The CAO's 2012 compliance audit of IFC investments in third-party financial intermediaries, and Inclusive Development International's 2016 report on the same portfolio.

title: Donors pay for the preparation inside the lender, and most of that money arrives tied to a named country
conviction: The lender's own trust fund report, read once. No test of whether the earmarking changed what was prepared.
summary:
Alongside its own capital, a development lender holds money that donors give it to spend. The World Bank Group's trust fund annual report for the 2024 financial year records US$17.8 billion of contributions to its trust funds and financial intermediary funds in that year, and US$35.1 billion in 2023. Sovereign governments provided 91 per cent, US$37.8 billion, of the cash contributions to the Bank's own trust funds over the 2020 to 2024 financial years. The United States was the largest single contributor at US$24.1 billion, then Germany at US$2.3 billion and the United Kingdom at US$2.0 billion.

Most of that money is not given for the Bank to allocate. Over the same five years, 76 per cent of the cash contributions to the Bank's own trust funds, US$31.5 billion of US$41.4 billion, was for country-specific purposes, primarily Ukraine, Afghanistan, Ethiopia, and the West Bank and Gaza. US$23.1 billion of the United States' US$24.1 billion was for trust funds supporting Ukraine alone. Part of the total is spent by the Bank itself rather than passed to a recipient: Bank-executed disbursing accounts paid out US$1.3 billion in the 2024 financial year, and about US$5.8 billion over the five years. That is the money that pays for studies, advice and project preparation. Trust funds supported 11 per cent of total World Bank disbursements for recipient-executed activities over the same five years.

The terms are the part that is not published. The Bank publishes totals by donor and by country type. The individual administration agreements, which say what the donor's money may and may not be used for, are not published alongside them.
implications: If it holds, then the choice of what gets studied and prepared is partly a donor's choice rather than the lender's, and a country with no donor interested in it gets no preparatory work, however large its need. It would also mean the figures a lender publishes about its own priorities describe money it did not direct. For this map it would mean the existing patterns on tied aid and on earmarked money to multilateral bodies have a third case: earmarking inside a development bank.
missing: Only one year's report has been read, and the figures are totals rather than a breakdown by activity. No administration agreement has been obtained. Nobody has checked whether the countries that received Bank-executed trust fund money went on to receive more lending than comparable countries that did not. Neither of the two existing patterns on earmarking covers this money: the pattern on tied aid is about which companies win contracts, and the pattern on earmarked multilateral money is about UN bodies, not development banks.
would_refute: The administration agreements turning out to leave the choice of activity to the lender, with the country label describing where the work was eventually done rather than a donor instruction. The agreements for the largest Bank-executed trust funds would show that.
would_settle: The administration agreements for the largest Bank-executed trust funds, with the lists of activities each one funded, set against the lending that followed in those countries.

countries.role: Largest named destination of earmarked contributions
countries.note: US$23.1 billion of the United States' US$24.1 billion of contributions over the 2020 to 2024 financial years went to trust funds supporting Ukraine. The map holds 8 Ukrainian cases, none of them about this money.

countries.role: Named destination of country-specific trust funds
countries.note: One of the four countries the report names as the main destinations of country-specific contributions. The map holds 15 Ethiopian cases, several of them road and project cases prepared with outside money.

countries.role: Named destination, and the largest umbrella disburser
countries.note: The report names Afghanistan among the main destinations of country-specific contributions and records the Afghanistan Resilience Trust Fund as the largest disbursing umbrella programme.

looked_at: The World Bank Group trust fund annual report covering the 2024 financial year, its financial tables and its figures 11, 13, 14 and 15.
